note: Derived from the mechanisms on these 78 cards and checked against FDA labeling where a claim was uncertain. It covers the interactions a fundamentals exam asks about and a nurse should recognize at the bedside. It is NOT a complete interaction screen and does not replace a pharmacy check or an interaction database.

severity_key.avoid: Do not combine without a specific, deliberate reason.
severity_key.high: Combine only with active monitoring; this is where patients get hurt.
severity_key.moderate: Usually manageable with timing, dose adjustment, or closer watching.

rules.name: Bleeding risk stacks
rules.mechanism:
Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.
rules.watch: Bruising, gum and nose bleeding, hematuria, tarry stool, new or worsening headache. H&H and platelets.
rules.exam: Two anticoagulants together is almost always wrong, EXCEPT a deliberate bridge: heparin or enoxaparin overlapping warfarin until the INR is therapeutic, or the 5-day parenteral lead-in dabigatran requires. Know the difference between a bridge and a duplication.

rules.name: Potassium climbs
rules.mechanism: ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.
rules.watch: Serum K⁺. ECG for peaked T waves, widening QRS, lost P waves. Muscle weakness.
rules.exam: Lisinopril plus Bactrim is the classic tested pair and a real cause of hospitalization. Hyperkalemia flattens the resting membrane potential until sodium channels can't reset, so the heart slows, blocks, and arrests.

rules.name: Potassium falls
rules.mechanism: Loop diuretics dump K⁺ at the loop of Henle. Prednisone and methylprednisolone hold Na⁺ and trade away K⁺ through mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone has almost none of that activity, so its hypokalemia is weaker and arrives by other routes at high dose. Insulin and sodium bicarbonate don't remove potassium at all, they drive it into cells, which looks identical on a lab draw.
rules.watch: K⁺ and Mg²⁺ together, because you cannot correct potassium while magnesium is low. ECG for U waves and ectopy.
rules.exam: This rule feeds the QT rule. Low K⁺ and low Mg²⁺ lengthen the QT on their own, so a patient on furosemide who then gets ondansetron is at far more torsades risk than either drug suggests alone.

rules.name: QT prolongation and torsades
rules.mechanism:
After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, ciprofloxacin and Bactrim are the established ones. For metronidazole the evidence is case reports, and fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat those two as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.
rules.watch: Baseline and follow-up ECG. Correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺ BEFORE giving, because correcting them is what actually lowers the risk.
rules.exam: Metronidazole's own label names the interaction: QT prolongation reported 'particularly when administered with drugs with the potential for prolonging the QT interval.' The common hospital version is a patient on furosemide receiving ondansetron plus a fluoroquinolone.

rules.name: Sedation and respiratory depression
rules.mechanism: Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep.
rules.watch: Respiratory rate and sedation level before AND after every dose. Sedation rises before the rate falls, so a rousable-but-drowsy patient is the warning, not the reassurance. Naloxone available.
rules.exam: Opioid plus benzodiazepine carries a black box on both drugs. Opioid plus gabapentinoid carries an FDA warning added in 2019. If a question hands you a patient on an opioid and lorazepam, respiratory status is the answer.

rules.name: Serotonin syndrome
rules.mechanism:
Too much serotonin at the synapse. Fluoxetine, venlafaxine and duloxetine raise it directly by blocking its reuptake, and methadone does the same weakly.

Ondansetron and metoclopramide are a different case. They BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising serotonin, and the link to serotonin syndrome rests on case reports with no established mechanism. Treat them as a reason to look, not a reason to expect it.
rules.watch: Agitation, hyperthermia, tachycardia, labile BP, HYPERREFLEXIA and clonus, diarrhea.
rules.exam: Hyperreflexia and clonus separate serotonin syndrome from NMS, which has lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia. Onset is hours, not days. A post-op patient on duloxetine who gets ondansetron is the realistic scenario.

rules.name: Acute kidney injury (the triple whammy)
rules.mechanism:
The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.
rules.watch: BUN, creatinine, eGFR, urine output, daily weight.
rules.exam: 'Triple whammy' is the actual name in the literature. It is one of the most common preventable causes of hospital-acquired AKI, and all three drugs are things a patient may already be taking for good reasons.

rules.name: Bradycardia and AV block
rules.mechanism: Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.
rules.watch: Apical pulse for a full minute, BP, ECG for PR interval and dropped beats.
rules.exam: Amlodipine is the safe CCB here, because it is vessel-selective and does nothing to the AV node. Verapamil is the most dangerous of the pair, and IV verapamil with an IV beta blocker can cause asystole.

rules.name: CYP3A4 inhibition raises drug levels
rules.mechanism: These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose.
rules.watch: Statin: new muscle pain, weakness, dark urine, CK. DOAC: any bleeding.
rules.exam: Diltiazem or verapamil with simvastatin is the textbook pair, and the simvastatin dose is capped at 10 mg because of it. Grapefruit juice belongs in the same bucket.

rules.name: CYP2D6 inhibition by fluoxetine
rules.mechanism: Fluoxetine AND bupropion are both potent CYP2D6 inhibitors. The fluoxetine metabolite norfluoxetine has a 4-16 day half-life, so the blockade persists for WEEKS after fluoxetine is stopped. For a drug cleared by 2D6, the level climbs. For a PRODRUG that needs 2D6 to be activated, the opposite happens: it never converts, so it stops working.
rules.watch: Pain relief that never arrives; or unexpected bradycardia.
rules.exam: This is the one interaction that makes a drug fail rather than overdose. Easy to miss because nothing looks wrong on the monitor.

rules.name: Phenytoin induces enzymes and strips other drugs
rules.mechanism: Phenytoin is a strong inducer of CYP enzymes and P-glycoprotein. It accelerates the clearance of a long list of drugs, so they drop below therapeutic levels at an unchanged dose.
rules.watch: Drug levels for phenytoin and valproate, INR for warfarin, and signs the other drug has simply stopped working.
rules.exam: The valproate-phenytoin pair is the subtle one. Nystagmus and ataxia in a patient whose total phenytoin level is 'fine' means check a FREE level and check albumin.

rules.name: Antibiotics push the INR up
rules.mechanism: Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole and Bactrim do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin (CYP2C9), so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those two push the INR hardest.
rules.watch: Recheck INR within a few days of starting OR stopping the antibiotic. Stopping it swings the INR back down.
rules.exam: Metronidazole and Bactrim are the two that spike the INR hardest. Any new antibiotic in a warfarin patient means an INR recheck, not a wait-and-see.

rules.name: Binders and cations block absorption
rules.mechanism: Divalent and trivalent cations chelate fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines in the gut, forming a complex that is never absorbed. Sevelamer is a polymer that binds far more than phosphate. Raising gastric pH changes absorption of drugs that need acid.
rules.watch: Treatment failure. The antibiotic level never gets high enough to work and nothing looks wrong at the bedside.
rules.exam: Separate by 2-6 hr. Sevelamer specifically: give other oral drugs 1 hr before or 3 hr after. This is a timing problem, not a do-not-combine problem.

rules.name: Dopamine blockers stack (EPS, NMS)
rules.mechanism: Both block central D2 receptors. Together the blockade deepens and so does every consequence of it.
rules.watch: Akathisia, acute dystonia, parkinsonian features, tardive dyskinesia, and NMS (fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered consciousness).
rules.exam: Akathisia gets mistaken for untreated nausea or anxiety, so the reflex is to give MORE antiemetic, which makes it worse. Treat acute dystonia with diphenhydramine or benztropine.

rules.name: GI ulceration and bleeding
rules.mechanism: NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would warn you. SSRIs add impaired platelet function on top.
rules.watch: Black or tarry stool, coffee-ground emesis, epigastric pain, falling H&H.
rules.exam: The steroid is what makes this dangerous, because it removes the warning pain. A patient on prednisone and ibuprofen can perforate without ever complaining of their stomach.

rules.name: NSAIDs blunt blood pressure drugs
rules.mechanism: Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.
rules.watch: BP creeping up, new edema, weight gain, a diuretic that stopped working.
rules.exam: If a question gives you a patient whose controlled BP suddenly isn't, look for a new over-the-counter NSAID before you look for nonadherence.

rules.name: Glucose control gets pushed both ways
rules.mechanism: Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and reduce peripheral glucose uptake, so insulin requirements rise, sometimes steeply. Beta blockers do something different and more dangerous: they mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (tremor, tachycardia) while sweating still comes through.
rules.watch: More frequent glucose checks. On a beta blocker, treat diaphoresis as hypoglycemia until proven otherwise.
rules.exam: Propranolol is the worst of the four, because nonselective blockade also blunts the glycogenolysis that would self-correct the low.

rules.name: Drugs that work against each other
rules.mechanism: Direct pharmacologic antagonism. One drug undoes what the other is for.
rules.watch: Ask why both are ordered. This is usually a reconciliation error rather than a plan.
rules.exam: Tranexamic acid is the only drug in this whole set whose job is to KEEP clot. Every anticoagulant and antiplatelet is its opposite.

rules.name: Muscle injury and rhabdomyolysis
rules.mechanism:
Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.
rules.watch: New muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness. CK. Dark or tea-colored urine means rhabdomyolysis, and creatinine next.
rules.exam: Ask about muscle symptoms at every visit, because patients write it off as having overdone it at the gym. The question that separates a complaint from an emergency is whether the urine is dark.

rules.name: Hidden acetaminophen (double dosing)
rules.mechanism:
Hydrocodone, oxycodone and codeine are usually dispensed as COMBINATION products that already contain acetaminophen. Norco, Percocet and Tylenol #3 all do.

So adding plain Tylenol on top is not a second drug. It is more of the same drug, arriving under a different name. The 4 g/day ceiling is the point where the liver starts to fail, not a suggestion, and many hospitals set their own limit at 3 g.
rules.watch: Add up acetaminophen from EVERY source: scheduled, PRN, combination opioids, and OTC cold products. Max 4 g/day, 3 g in chronic alcohol use or hepatic impairment.
rules.exam: This is the most common real-world acetaminophen overdose, and it happens to patients who were following instructions. If a question lists Percocet and Tylenol on the same MAR, that is the answer.

rules.name: Specific pairs worth knowing
rules.mechanism: Individual interactions that do not belong to a larger class.
rules.watch: Depends on the pair; each one names its own.
rules.exam: Allopurinol plus a penicillin is the sleeper here, because the consequence is a false allergy label that narrows every future antibiotic choice.

rules.name: Duplicate therapy
rules.mechanism: Two drugs doing the same job by the same mechanism. The effect doubles while the benefit does not, and on a med list it almost always means a reconciliation error rather than a plan.
rules.watch: Ask why both are on the list. This is a med-reconciliation finding more often than a prescribing one.
rules.exam: Duplicate therapy is its own category of error, separate from interaction. The ketorolac pairs are the ones with an actual labeled contraindication behind them.

rules.name: P-glycoprotein inhibition raises dabigatran
rules.mechanism:
Most drug interactions run through liver enzymes called CYP. Dabigatran does not use them at all. It depends instead on a pump in the gut wall, P-glycoprotein, that limits how much of the drug gets absorbed.

Block that pump and more dabigatran gets in, so the bleeding risk climbs. It also means dabigatran slips past every interaction warning built around liver enzymes, which is the real danger: nothing flags it.
rules.watch: Any bleeding, and renal function, since the risk concentrates at low CrCl.
rules.exam: If a question asks why dabigatran is different from apixaban and rivaroxaban pharmacokinetically, this is the answer: P-gp, not CYP3A4.

rules.name: Fluoroquinolones disturb glucose
rules.mechanism: Fluoroquinolones interfere with pancreatic beta-cell potassium channel regulation and can provoke severe hypoglycemia. The FDA required every systemic fluoroquinolone label to carry the risk of hypoglycemic coma, naming diabetic patients already on glucose-lowering drugs.
rules.watch: More frequent glucose checks for the duration of the antibiotic course. Risk concentrates in older adults.
rules.exam: Both directions have been reported, but hypoglycemia is the one that carries the FDA warning.

rules.why: Tylenol #3 is codeine WITH acetaminophen.
Norco and Vicodin are hydrocodone WITH acetaminophen. Adding Tylenol stacks an invisible dose.
Percocet is oxycodone WITH acetaminophen. Plain oxycodone exists too, so you have to read which one was dispensed.
Sustained acetaminophen (more than ~2 g/day for several days) raises the INR. A single dose does not.
Both inhibit xanthine oxidase. There is no reason to use both.

This IS done deliberately for active bleeding in an anticoagulated patient (dental surgery, trauma), so the question is not whether to allow it but whether an indication exists. On a routine med list with no bleeding, it is a reconciliation error.
Labeled contraindication: ketorolac is contraindicated in patients currently receiving aspirin.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.

Loop diuretics dump K⁺ at the loop of Henle. Prednisone and methylprednisolone hold Na⁺ and trade away K⁺ through mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone has almost none of that activity, so its hypokalemia is weaker and arrives by other routes at high dose. Insulin and sodium bicarbonate don't remove potassium at all, they drive it into cells, which looks identical on a lab draw.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. An ACE inhibitor or ARB WITH a loop diuretic is guideline-directed therapy in heart failure, not an error. It becomes the triple whammy only when an NSAID joins. Monitor creatinine; do not treat the pair itself as a problem.

Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep. Common and appropriate, since opioids themselves cause nausea. The caution is additive sedation, not that the pair is wrong.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.
